The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(-1,0)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$ The point $B$ has coordinates $(0,-1)$ and lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ If ${f}^{′}(-1)=3,$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0)?$

$({f}^{-1})^{′}(0)=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Since $B\,(0,-1)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(0)=-1.$
We're also told that ${f}^{′}(-1)=3.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
